snippet (ordered basic to deeper within: A commit is a saved snapshot of the whole project with a message saying why. It stays on this Mac until pushed, and you can always go back to it.
Small commits are easier to review and easier to undo. If one change breaks something, you can reverse just that one instead of losing a day's work.
Git has a waiting area called the staging area or index. You choose what goes in, and the commit saves exactly that. tools/hs save puts everything in, then commits.
Git hooks are scripts git runs at set moments. Ours run before each commit and can refuse it, which is how an unapproved plan blocks code.
Every commit has an ID such as 1e545b90, calculated from its content. Change anything and the ID changes, so history can't be quietly altered.
A branch is a separate line of work. You can experiment without touching main, and main only changes when finished work is merged in.
A branch is only a label pointing at a commit, so creating one is instant. That is why one branch per task costs nothing.
main is the single trusted version. Keeping every task on its own short-lived branch means main always holds finished, reviewed work.
The longer a branch lives, the further it drifts from main and the harder it is to merge. That is why tools/hs status shows each open task's age.
A merge brings the commits from one branch into another. A merge commit has two parents, which records that two lines of work joined there.
A conflict means two branches changed the same lines and git won't guess which is right. Nothing is lost; a person chooses the final text.
Merging main into a task branch brings across what happened on main since the branch began, so the task isn't working from old information.
Push copies your commits to GitHub. Until then the work exists only on this Mac, so pushing is also your off-site backup.
Push sends commits to GitHub and pull fetches them back. Git is distributed: your Mac and GitHub each hold the full history.
A force-push overwrites history on GitHub and can destroy other people's work. That is why it's blocked here; fixes go in as new commits instead.
Pull is two steps: fetch downloads new commits, then merge combines them with your branch. Fetch alone is always safe, because it changes none of your files.
A tag is a permanent name for one commit. Unlike a branch it never moves, so handover/site-search-2026-11-06 always means that exact version.
Drift is when what's running on live no longer matches what's in the repo. It happens here because Nick can edit live directly, so we compare before each task.
A source of truth is the one place you trust when copies disagree. Ours is split: git for our changes, the live export for what's actually running.
A backup you have never restored from is only a hope. rollback/ in each package holds the files from the real live export, so the route back is ready before you deploy.
A release package is a fixed bundle of exactly what changes, plus how to undo it. The person deploying doesn't have to work out what's needed.
Plan the undo before the deploy. A rollback written beforehand takes minutes; working it out during an outage is when mistakes happen.
Dev, staging and production are separate copies of a system. Our Local site is dev and live is production, so some files, like the loader, must never cross over.
Deploying means putting code where real users get it. It is separate from merging, which is why DEPLOY-LOG.md only records what was confirmed live.
Caches keep copies of pages to serve them faster, so visitors can see old content after a deploy. That is why we purge WP Super Cache and Cloudflare.
A smoke test is a quick check straight after a deploy that the main things still work. It doesn't prove everything, but it catches the disasters early.
A linter reads code without running it and flags mistakes. php -l catches syntax errors that would otherwise take the whole site down.
Passing lint only means the code can be read, not that it does the right thing. That is why lint is followed by tests and UAT.
HTTP status codes are a server's short answer: 200 is OK, 301 and 302 are redirects, 404 is not found, and 5xx means the server failed.
A 301 says moved permanently, so browsers may remember it. A 302 says temporary and asks each time, which is why share links use 302: every click reaches us.
The part of a URL after ? is the query string. UTM tags live there, so any redirect that doesn't pass it along loses them.
WP-CLI runs WordPress tasks from the command line. Commands are repeatable and can be scripted, unlike clicking through wp-admin.
WordPress hooks let code run at set moments without editing core files. add_action does something at a moment; add_filter changes a value passing through.
parse_request runs before WordPress fetches the page's content from the database. Share links use it so they can redirect without doing that work.
Never paste a visitor's input straight into SQL. $wpdb->prepare keeps data apart from commands, which is the standard defence against SQL injection.
Escape data when you output it. esc_html and esc_attr turn special characters into harmless text, so stored data can't run as code in a browser.
Reading a number, adding one and saving it can lose clicks if two arrive together. A single SQL UPDATE does all three as one step, which is called atomic.
WordPress runs all plugin code in one shared space, so two functions with the same name crash the site. That's why ours all begin with hs_.
PHP runs on the server before the page is sent. JavaScript runs afterwards in the visitor's browser, so it can react to clicks but can't be trusted for security.
Event listeners run code when something happens, such as a click. Listening on a parent element also covers items added to the page later.
CSS applies by specificity and order: a more specific rule wins, and on a tie the later one does. Most surprises come from a rule you can't see winning.
A hook is automation that can't forget. CLAUDE.md is advice that could be overlooked, while a hook always runs and can block an action.
An idempotent command gives the same result however many times it runs. tools/hs setup is built that way, so running it twice is safe.
Put checks where they can't be skipped. A rule enforced at the commit stage holds whichever tool made the change, not just the one you remembered to set up.
A plan is the cheapest place to change your mind. Fixing a design takes minutes in a document and days once it's in code and on live.
A gate is a checkpoint that work must pass before moving on. Each one here checks something different: plan, code, behaviour, package, then live.
Most design choices trade one good thing for another. Writing down what you gave up, and why, stops the same debate returning six months later.
